name: Freya Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a crew that mostly builds connections for new solar farms and battery sites in the uplands, so it's new line, new poles, a lot of mud. We meet at the yard at half six, I check the day's route on my phone while the others are finding their gloves, and then it's an hour's drive to wherever the site is. I'm an apprentice, so I'm rigging, hauling cable, setting up the stringing gear, and doing my first proper climbs. I love that the things we build will be there in forty years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What brought you to it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ran a café for eight years on the high street in our town, the Copper Kettle, and it went under after the energy prices and the rent went up together. We're still paying off the loan. I wanted a job with a wage that came every month, and building the grid felt like the opposite of a café, useful in a way people can't scroll past. What wears me out is the cold, and being slow at things my body hasn't learned yet. Mats is a primary school teacher, so we're fine on paper and broke in real life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, so it's a good assistant and not a revolution, that's still useful. At work I'd probably get teased, because I'm the one always asking the chatbot things. Online I'd say something like, great, now let's use it for the boring stuff and get on with life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means I keep doing what I'm doing. I finish my apprenticeship, use AI to help me study and keep our budget straight, and we chip away at the café loan. Nothing big changes, which is honestly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on with the apprenticeship, two and a half years left. Keep using AI to quiz me on theory and to work out the cheapest way to pay down the loan. Maybe start a little side thing doing bookkeeping for other small businesses with AI help, a few evenings a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use AI now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every day. I use it to explain the regulations, to plan the drive to the site, to sort out our bills. When I had the café, it did my rotas and my stock orders, which saved me hours. I'd be lost without it now, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a plateau change your plans at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. My plan's to finish my ticket and get our heads above water. If AI stays a handy tool, that just helps.

S0.say: She'd say AI as a good assistant is still useful, and online she'd suggest using it for the boring stuff and getting on with life. At work she'd expect teasing for always asking the chatbot.
S0.think: I keep doing what I'm doing: finish my apprenticeship, use AI to study and budget, and chip away at the café loan. Nothing big changes, and that's fine.
S0.do: Carries on with her apprenticeship, which has two and a half years left, using AI for theory and to plan loan payments. Considers a small evening side business doing AI-assisted bookkeeping for small businesses.
S0.quote: When I had the café, it did my rotas and my stock orders, which saved me hours. I'd be lost without it now, honestly.
S0.fieldNote: Freya is a heavy AI user who ran her café's rotas and stock with it. The café debt, not technology, is what keeps her thin. Even in a plateau she's already thinking of a small bookkeeping side business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, okay, let's be the people who get good at it first. At work I'd volunteer for anything new. With friends I'd say don't wait for someone to train you, the tools are free, learn them now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this could be good for me. I'm not the strongest climber and I never will be, but I'm good with the new stuff. If the job becomes more about drones, sensors and planning, I'd have an edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Within a month I'd ask the company about drone and sensor courses, and do free online courses in the evenings. Start using AI tools to plan our crew's jobs, if the foreman lets me. And keep the bookkeeping side thing going, because it's more income and a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly. A little nervous about money, but mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks on your crew might change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The surveying for new lines, the planning, the fault checks. Maybe the stringing gear gets smarter. The climbing and the actual joining of cables, that's people for a while yet, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've run a business. Does that shape how you see this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. When the café was going under I learned you have to move before you're forced to. I waited too long with the café, kept hoping the rent would come down. I wouldn't do that again.

S1.say: She'd say let's be the people who get good at it first, volunteer for anything new at work, and tell friends the tools are free, so learn them now.
S1.think: This could be good for me. I'm not the strongest climber, but if the job becomes drones, sensors and planning, I'd have an edge.
S1.do: Asks the company about drone and sensor courses within a month and takes free online courses in the evenings. Offers to use AI to plan crew jobs and keeps her bookkeeping side income going.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, with some nerves about money.
S1.quote: I waited too long with the café, kept hoping the rent would come down. I wouldn't do that again.
S1.fieldNote: The café's failure taught Freya to move before she's forced, and gradual change looks like an opening to her. She knows she'll never be the strongest climber and sees new tools as her edge. Her side income doubles as a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready, so let's not pretend we are, and let's work out what we can actually do. At work I'd say get any training you can before it's gone. Online I'd share practical stuff, like how to talk to your bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me. I'm an apprentice with a café loan and less than a month of savings, and two years is nothing. Being good with AI doesn't help when AI's doing all the jobs, including bookkeeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, ring the bank about the café loan and the mortgage before we fall behind. Grab any bridge job I can, like helping companies install and set up the robots, because they'll need people for a while. And cut everything we can: the car, the kids' clubs, takeaways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the café's last month, but bigger and with no lease to end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Elsa and Theo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth, that things would be tight, but that their mum is good at starting over. Elsa's thirteen, she'd want details, so I'd give her some. Theo would want to know if he can still have hot chocolate on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're comfortable with risk. Does that help here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, because I'd move fast and not sit frozen. But risk needs a cushion, and we don't have one. Last time I took a risk, it cost us the café and a loan we're still paying.

S2.say: She'd say nobody's ready, so let's work out what can actually be done, urge the crew to get training while it's available, and share practical tips online like how to talk to the bank.
S2.think: It scares me: an apprentice with a café loan and less than a month saved. Being good with AI doesn't help when AI is doing all the jobs, including bookkeeping.
S2.do: Calls the bank in the first month about the café loan and mortgage before falling behind. Looks for a bridge job helping companies install and set up robots and cuts the car, kids' clubs and takeaways.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like the café's last month but bigger.
S2.quote: Being good with AI doesn't help when AI's doing all the jobs, including bookkeeping.
S2.fieldNote: Freya's usual confidence meets her lack of cushion here, and her side income would vanish too. She'd still move fast, chasing a bridge job setting up robots. She knows risk needs a cushion and she has none.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you're smart about it. At work I'd tell people to start learning the robot side now. With friends I'd say make a plan this year, not in year four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I finish my ticket and get in early on the robot work. I think I could become the person who sets up and checks the robot crews, at least for a few years. After that, honestly, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the apprenticeship in two and a half years, and do robotics and automation courses on the side, online, starting this winter. Keep the bookkeeping going and save every bit of it toward the loan. And ask the company to put me on the team that trials new kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more curious than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'd be grabbing whatever's floating. Five years, I can actually steer. That's a big difference for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about running a business again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If I could start a small company that installs and maintains robots on solar sites, with a couple of other ex-lineworkers, I'd do it. But only once the loan's paid. I'm not doing that again on borrowed money.

S3.say: She'd say five years is enough to get ready if you're smart, tell the crew to learn the robot side now, and urge friends to make a plan this year.
S3.think: Five years means I finish my ticket and get in early on robot work, maybe as the person who sets up and checks robot crews. After that I don't know.
S3.do: Finishes her apprenticeship and takes online robotics and automation courses from this winter. Saves her bookkeeping income toward the loan and asks to join the team that trials new kit.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but more curious than scared.
S3.quote: Two years, I'd be grabbing whatever's floating. Five years, I can actually steer.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Freya room to steer, and she'd use it to get onto the robot side early. She is tempted by another business, installing robots on solar sites, but only once the café loan is gone. Her honesty about not seeing past 2031 stands out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so let's not panic, let's plan. At work I'd say learn everything you can about the new kit. Online I'd be the annoying one posting course links.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I think I'd be fine, maybe better than fine. I'd be qualified, I'd know the robot side, and the loan would be gone. I could actually build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish my ticket, pay off the café loan in three or four years, and then start saving toward a small business, robot installation and maintenance for solar and battery sites. Keep learning, keep using AI to plan everything. And help Elsa think about what she wants to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually. Even a little excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you like to be in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running a little outfit with a couple of robot crews and a couple of people, doing maintenance on the solar farms we built. Not getting rich, just steady. And home for dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want to own robots. Isn't that the thing taking the jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. But someone's going to own them, and I'd rather it was a local person who hires local people than some company three countries away. That's how I see it.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is plenty, so plan rather than panic, tell the crew to learn the new kit, and be the one posting course links online.
S4.think: With ten years I'd be fine, maybe better than fine: qualified, trained on the robot side and free of the loan, so I could build something.
S4.do: Finishes her ticket and pays off the café loan in three or four years. Then saves toward a small robot installation and maintenance business for solar and battery sites, using AI to plan.
S4.quote: Someone's going to own them, and I'd rather it was a local person who hires local people than some company three countries away.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Freya flips from victim to owner: she imagines running a small robot maintenance outfit. When the contradiction was named, she answered that local ownership beats distant ownership. Her café experience shows in her caution about debt.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no cushion and no time to turn around. What would help is some kind of bridge money, like a few months of wages while you retrain, and loans for small businesses that don't need your house as security. I'd also like the banks to pause loan payments for people who lose their jobs to this.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about debt. Everyone talks about savings, but for a lot of us it's not that we have no savings, it's that we're still paying off the last disaster. The Copper Kettle closed three years ago and I'm still paying for the coffee machine.

headlineQuote: The Copper Kettle closed three years ago and I'm still paying for the coffee machine.
portrait: Freya Larsen is a 43-year-old apprentice lineworker building connections for new solar farms and battery sites, who came to the trade after her café, the Copper Kettle, went under. She and her partner Mats, a primary school teacher, have two kids, a mortgage and a café loan, and less than a month saved. She uses AI every day and learned from the café to move before she's forced. She is calm through the plateau and gradual change, alarmed when AGI arrives in two years and her cushion and side income vanish together, and steadily more hopeful at five and ten years, when she pictures running a small, local robot maintenance outfit.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd have no cushion and no time to turn around.
whatWouldHelp: Bridge money to cover a few months of wages while retraining, small-business loans that don't need a house as security, and paused loan payments for people who lose work to AI.
